title: Buster Posey keeps taking big swings as Giants president. When will they connect?
content:
The Patrick Bailey trade, like Buster Posey’s other big swings as San Francisco Giants president of baseball operations, is perfectly defensible in a vacuum. But the sum total of Posey’s moves, from the signing of Willy Adames to the trade for Rafael Devers to the hiring of Tony Vitello, is amounting to subtraction by addition.

The Giants are last in the majors in walks, tied for last in home runs and at 16-24, nearly last in the NL West. Netting the equivalent of a first-round pick plus a left-handed pitching prospect for Bailey, a catcher hitting .146, ultimately might prove to be a steal. Still, why were the Cleveland Guardians celebrating the trade as if they had just won the draft lottery?

Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said he received texts from eight or nine members of the Giants organization raving about Bailey. President of baseball operations Chris Antonetti said Baltimore Orioles manager Craig Albernaz, the former Giants catching coach and Guardians bench coach, asked him, “Now you acquire him, after I leave?”

The Guardians are forever challenged offensively, so in that sense, acquiring Bailey to go with their other all-glove, no-bat catcher, Austin Hedges, is on brand. When it comes to run prevention, however, few teams are better than Cleveland. So, when the Guardians renewed their longstanding quest to acquire Bailey, shouldn’t it have given Posey pause?

No front office is perfect. In November 2021, the Guardians made what looks like an all-time blunder, trading Junior Caminero for Tobias Myers. But the Guardians, at least, are content to accept Bailey for who he is. The best defensive catcher in the game. And not by a small margin.

Posey, over time, grew frustrated with Bailey, according to people familiar with their relationship. A three-time World Series champion at catcher, Posey valued running a pitching staff over some of Bailey’s best attributes — throwing and framing and understanding advanced metrics. The latter two skills, in particular, are valued more in today’s game than when Posey played.

Perhaps a tipping point for Posey occurred in Game 1 of a doubleheader at Philadelphia on April 30, when Bailey, in the ninth inning, called for reliever Ryan Walker to throw nine straight sinkers to Bryson Stott. Stott tied the score with a double, and the Giants got walked off in both that game and the next one as well, with reliever Keaton Winn at one point throwing 10 straight splitters.

Bailey’s .396 OPS alone was enough to drive Posey to distraction, particularly when the rest of the Giants also were struggling offensively. But once Daniel Susac comes off the injured list, the Giants will bank on a catching combination of Susac, a Rule 5 pick who had small-sample success at the start of the season; Jesus Rodriguez, a rookie acquired in the Camilo Doval trade who probably fits best as a utility man; and Eric Haase, a 33-year-old journeyman.

Posey emphasizes pitching and defense, yet he just traded one of the game’s top defenders. The Giants’ remaining catchers are not nearly as strong defensively. Susac, who now seems to be something of a great hope, was left unprotected by the Athletics. And here’s guessing Bailey will hit better playing in a more forgiving ballpark, a more forgiving division and, considering how Posey soured on him, a more forgiving organization.

The flip side — the coup Posey pulled off by acquiring the Guardians’ competitive balance pick, No. 29 overall — is also clear. The Giants already hold the fourth overall selection. The slot value of the 29th pick increased their pool to $17.35 million, the fourth highest in the draft. The larger a team’s pool, the more it can maneuver with picks in negotiations.

The Giants’ system, ranked No. 13 by The Athletic’s Keith Law, already is on the rise. The two top 30 picks could add to their momentum — though, of course, the draft offers no guarantees. The Giants, remember, took Bailey 13th overall in 2020.

Posey was once part of a fantastic homegrown core. He wants to build another. At this point, it’s almost a necessity. The Giants’ big three — Devers, Adames and Matt Chapman — are on pace to hit 32 homers. Not individually. Combined.

As if that’s not bad enough, the Giants’ 5.4 percent walk rate through Saturday would make them the first team since the 1966 St. Louis Cardinals to finish below 6 percent. This, at a time when the Automated Ball-Strike (ABS) challenge system has led to a significant jump in the league’s overall walk rate, from 8.4 percent last season to 9.5 percent.

Some of this — most of it, actually — is on the players. Devers’ walk rate has fallen from 15.4 percent to 5.7, Chapman’s from 13.3 to 9.4, Adames’ from 11.7 to 3.8. Most of the Giants’ other regulars never walked much to begin with. And the new manager, Vitello, and hitting coach from the contact-oriented Toronto Blue Jays, Hunter Mense, sure don’t seem to have the answers to the problem.

The days of managers flipping over clubhouse spreads to get their players’ attention are over. Skippers, though, can get their messages across in other ways. The Arizona Diamondbacks’ Torey Lovullo recently met with his starting pitchers, imploring them to throw more strikes. The meeting, in which Lovullo also allowed each of the pitchers to have their say, sparked immediate improvement.

Perhaps Lovullo should try the same thing with his hitters, whose walk rate through Saturday ranked ahead of only the Giants. Lovullo is in his 10th season. His words carry weight. Vitello, working in Major League Baseball for the first time after coaching at the University of Tennessee, might one day be a very good manager. But at this stage of his career, he cannot possibly possess the same type of credibility with his players.

Posey, hired in September 2024, is also relatively new to his job. Unlike, say, the New York Mets’ David Stearns, he has no track record of success. His fearlessness and decisiveness stand out in an industry in which most executives are risk-averse. And his desire to add Adames and Devers, after the Giants’ repeated whiffs in free agency, from Bryce Harper and Aaron Judge to Shohei Ohtani and Yoshinobu Yamamoto, was understandable. (Before taking over, Posey also played a key role in negotiating Chapman’s extension.)

Adames has never made an All-Star team, never won a Gold Glove or Silver Slugger award. His seven-year, $182 million free-agent contract, the largest in team history, was considered a mild overpay upon its completion in December 2024, a year too long. But then, as now, Adames’ $26 million average annual value was not terribly out of line for a shortstop of his caliber.

Devers had $255 million remaining on his deal when Posey acquired him last June, but he was 28 at the time, seemingly with his best years ahead of him. The Boston Red Sox surely are gleeful they escaped the contract but should hold off on any victory dance. They botched their communication with Devers. They haven’t recovered from losing the hitter they had. And they appear to have moved on prematurely from two players they acquired in the deal, left-hander Kyle Harrison and outfielder James Tibbs III.

By securing Chapman, Adames, and Devers, Posey showed the Giants could land quality performers, if not elite stars. Now the team must live with the consequences of committing nearly $600 million to those players, all of whom might have peaked.

Few, though, expected the Giants’ offense to be this bad. If anything, their bigger concern was pitching. Posey’s only upgrades to the rotation were Tyler Mahle (5.18 ERA) and Adrian Houser (6.19 ERA). He barely touched his bullpen, which on Sunday underwent a shakeup that included the demotion of Walker, who entered the season as the front-runner to be the team’s closer.

This isn’t what the Giants or their fans envisioned. Fans grew weary of the teams constructed by Posey’s predecessor, Farhan Zaidi, pining for greater roster continuity, bigger names. Posey has delivered on both those fronts, and still the team isn’t successful. So now, he’s scrambling.

In the past week alone, the Giants have promoted top prospect Bryce Eldridge along with Rodriguez, traded Bailey and overhauled their bullpen. Operation Save the Season is in full effect, but how long before the Posey Plan, too, must be abandoned?

How long before fans ask, what’s next?
